editorialDecl.p: Modern English translation based on the normalized modern Spanish version. Las Casas wrote this chapter almost entirely in Latin, noting that he set it down in Latin so that learned men might read and correct it. All prose has been translated into English. Canon law and civil law citations have been retained in Latin.

div.head: Chapter 11
div.p: Chapter 11. From the preceding fifth principle, the sixth follows. And this one is set down in Latin, so that learned men may read it, and correct it if they see fit. Sixth Principle.

In order that our illustrious kings may rightly, that is, in accordance with the laws and with due circumstances, acquire just possession of the supreme principality of the Indies, it is necessarily required that the consent of the kings and peoples of the said world intervene, such that they freely consent to the institution or donation made of our kings by the Apostolic See.

This principle is proved in multiple ways. First, thus: the Apostolic See through the said institution or donation did not deprive those peoples of their dominions, dignities, royal prerogatives, states, and jurisdictions, chiefly because these are known to belong to them by natural law and the law of nations, as appeared from the preceding principle; therefore it did not deprive them of their liberty or of those things that pertain to liberty, because liberty is not well exchanged for all the gold in the world, since it has no estimation, as in L. libertas, ff., De regulis iuris. For liberty is a natural faculty, that is, the possibility of doing what one pleases, save what is prohibited by force or by law. Servitude, however, is that by which someone is subjected against nature to another's dominion, as in L. libertas, ff., De statu hominum. Now, what pertains above all to liberty is to consent or not consent to a foreign king or dominion, since thereby free kings and peoples are reduced to servitude: kings, because they must recognize a superior, which is for kings naturally the greatest horror; and peoples, because they are forced to suffer a double and harsher servitude. And this is the greatest prejudice to both. For subjection and the oath of fealty are a kind of servitude, and one who is under the jurisdiction of another is said to be as it were that person's slave, as in ff., De usufructuario, L. si usufructus, 15; et L. cum servum, ad fin. et ibi Doctores, Codex, De servis fugitivis; et in c. cum olim, el 2.º de privilegio. It is necessary that all those who are prejudiced consent together and freely, as in cap. cum omnes, De constitutionibus, in the rule "What touches all," De regulis iuris, Lib. VI. Therefore, in order that our illustrious kings may rightly and justly acquire just possession of the supreme principality of the Indies, it is necessarily required that the consent of the kings and peoples of the said world intervene, etc.

It is likewise proved in the second place: those kingdoms and peoples of that entire world were free by natural law and the law of nations at the time we found them, having kings and princes, recognizing no superior outside themselves either in law or in fact, as has been said, exercising full and pure authority and all power and jurisdiction, just as other kings of the world do. For that new world, in the vast ocean sea, is most remote from every region that men have ever known, occupied and possessed by those Indians from time immemorial, and we found and saw with our own eyes that their own natural kings reigned over it, and so were entirely exempt or free from every superior. This is proved by ff., De iustitia et iure, L. ex hoc iure, where it says: "peoples were distinguished, kingdoms founded, dominions set apart." Where it appears that those peoples and their kings were free, recognizing no superior, by natural law and the law of nations. Therefore without their free consent and goodwill, another new king cannot be given to them. Otherwise violence and most grievous injury and the most enormous harm would be done to them, if we were to subject free kings and subjects, lords and vassals, to servitude against nature and reason. And consequently such a principality would be violent, usurped, and tyrannical, as is proved by C. 1 q. 1, c. principatus; et L. decernimus, Codex, De sacrosanctis ecclesiis. See Baldo, above in chapter IV.

Since, therefore, it was not the intention of the supreme vicar of Christ to inflict prejudice upon the liberty and rights of the kings and peoples of that world, or to bring violence to bear upon them in any way, or injury, or to grant license for others to inflict it, or to approve what had already been inflicted, it is manifest that the supreme vicar of Christ understood and willed that, in order for our kings to rightly and justly acquire just possession of the supreme principality of that world, the goodwill of the kings and peoples of the said world should be sought, such that they freely consent to the papal institution or donation made of our kings.

It is likewise proved in the third place thus: whenever a free man, and still more a free people or community, must be bound to bear some burden or to discharge some debt, and in general when the prejudice of many is at stake, it is necessary to summon all those whom it touches and to obtain their free consent. Otherwise nothing that is done will be valid, as is sufficiently clear among those learned in the law. But if the king of Spain, insofar as he is king of Castile and León, were imposed upon the Indian nations and their princes as their universal or supreme king and lord, in law or in fact, they would be bound at least civilly, as regards the judicial forum or human judgment, to the most grievous burden and to the discharge of an intolerable debt: namely, to recognize as their king and lord a man wholly unknown to them, king of another, foreign, barbarous, and at first sight very suspect nation, and therefore to render him obedience, subjection, reverence, revenues, tributes, services, new impositions, and the other royal dues; from which there would follow an incomparable and perhaps irreparable harm. Therefore it is necessary to summon all the kings and peoples of those nations, and to await and obtain from them their free consent. All of this is plain. For it is well known in law that all those whom a matter principally touches must be cited, as in the rule of law: "and it must be approved or rejected by all," namely all those who are harmed, or whose right is diminished, or who are prejudiced, to whom the power of consenting or dissenting has been given by natural, divine, and human law, as Baldo says in L. nam ita demum, ff., De adoptionibus, et the Gloss; from which he draws the argument that when rescripts are sought, those who would be harmed by the rescript must intervene: ff., De natalibus restituendis, L. filium; et ff., De minoribus, L. in causae cognitione, causa; et in Autbent., Ut sponsalitia largitas, cap. ad hec, Collatio 8.

All the foregoing is proved and confirmed also in the fourth place: because it is found so ordained in Sacred Scripture, that in the granting and constitution of a new and supreme prince from the beginning, and even of the prince whom God had designated or chosen, the free consent and authority, or voluntary acceptance of the people, must intervene, without which even the divine institution of the supreme prince took no effect. This is clear from Deuteronomy 17, where it is said: "When you shall say: I will set a king over me, as all the nations that are round about me have, you shall set him over you whom the Lord your God shall choose, etc." In which words the Lord decreed and commanded that two things must concur for the just institution of a king. The one, on the part of the one to be instituted: namely, that he shall have been chosen by divine Providence, awaiting in the election the judgment of God. The other, on the part of the people: namely, that the people should voluntarily receive and willingly ratify the one elected by God as king, and deliver to him the possession of the kingdom. Which two things the aforesaid words sufficiently denote: "you shall set over you him whom God shall choose"; where a voluntary act was required, that is, the consent and approval of the people in "you shall set over you," that is, you shall ratify and accept, and shall have as king the one whom God shall have given to be understood as chosen. Wherefore, although God could have set a king over the Hebrew people even without their consent, being Lord of all, Hebrews 1 and Daniel 4, he was nonetheless unwilling to deprive that people of the privilege of natural law which pertains to all men and to every free people: to submit of their own free will to another's governance if they see it to be useful to them. For God does not destroy or abrogate his own work or the natural law which from the beginning he himself instituted so wisely, so orderly, and so immutably. For it is not the character of divine providence to force or corrupt natures; and the great Dionysius, lib. 4, De divinis nominibus, says that he "preserves" them. Wherefore, just as by divine ordination it had the force of a precept that the people should voluntarily set over themselves as king the one whom the Lord should choose — that is, ratify such an election of God and deliver to him the possession of the kingdom — so by the same just divine ordination the consent of the people, the ratification, and the delivery of possession of the kingdom were necessarily required for the exercise of royal power. For if God did not require this consent of the people, he would simply have said: "He shall be king over you whom the Lord shall choose"; and it would not have been necessary to add: "You shall set over you him whom the Lord shall choose, etc." For the words of Sacred Scripture must be weighed carefully, since it is full of mysteries, and it would be wrong to suppose that anything improper, superfluous, or deficient could be found in it. This indeed is also clearly evident in the two first kings, Saul and David, of the people of Israel. For as is recorded in 1 Kings, chapter 10, although Saul had first been anointed by the command of God through Samuel as king, and through that anointing had obtained right and title to that kingdom, it was nonetheless afterwards necessary that he be instituted and accepted by the people as king, and that the possession of the kingdom be delivered to him. For he did not dare to exercise jurisdiction or the authority of royal power, nor could he do so with full right, before the people had consented to the election made of him and had delivered or granted him possession of the kingdom, as is plain there; see there again.

The same you will find in 2 Kings, namely David, who although he had also been anointed as king by the prophet Samuel by the command of God, as in 1 Kings, chapter 16, nonetheless did not dare to involve himself in the exercise of royal power immediately after the death of Saul, nor did he assume the kingdom to himself, though he knew perfectly well that he had been elected and anointed by God for the kingdom of that people by his command; not being unaware that by divine precept he was to be constituted and enthroned in the kingdom by the consent and authority of the people: first, at Hebron, through the tribe of Judah — the men of Judah came, it says, and anointed David there to reign over Judah, 2 Kings, chapter 2 — and then, second, all the tribes of Israel came, and the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and he made a covenant with them at Hebron before the Lord, and they anointed David king over Israel, etc. This in chapter 5.

Behold how David, beyond the divine institution, promotion, and anointing, needed the approval and acceptance and delivery of possession of the kingdom through the free consent of the whole people, in order to have a legitimate and juridical entry into the kingdom; that is, to obtain rightly and justly the possession and exercise of royal power in that kingdom. Therefore, by the example of the divine law, in order for our kings to rightly and justly obtain just possession of the supreme principality of the world of the Indies, the institution, promotion, or donation alone of the Most Holy Apostolic See does not suffice, but it is necessarily required that the consent of the kings and peoples of those nations intervene, such that they freely consent to the said institution, promotion, or donation made of our kings by the same Holy See. On this, see more fully our treatise in the book De thesauris, chapter 22 and following. And thus the sixth principle is made plain.
